title: Canada looks through energy inflation as core prices and demand stay subdued
summary: The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% on 10 June, with the Bank Rate at 2.50% and the deposit rate at 2.20%. Two pieces of news had moved away from the April forecast in opposite directions. Oil was roughly $10 a barrel above the assumption in the April Monetary Policy Report, increasing near-term inflation pressure. Canadian first-quarter GDP, meanwhile, had edged down 0.1%, weaker than expected. Council judged that the economy would still have excess supply even if growth resumed in the second quarter. Its choice to leave the rate unchanged rested on whether higher energy costs were spreading through prices, not on how close the next headline CPI reading would be to 3%.

The 2.8% April inflation rate had two energy-related drivers. Oil was more expensive. In addition, the earlier elimination of the consumer carbon tax was dropping out of the twelve-month comparison. The second mechanism changes the annual growth rate because the price decline in the comparison period is no longer counted. It does not require a fresh tax increase in April. Those distinctions matter for persistence. A one-off change in the comparison base eventually passes; cost increases that reach new categories at different times can keep a broader measure elevated. The Bank projected headline inflation near 3% in the short term and a gradual return towards 2%, conditional on how those forces evolved (inflation paragraph).

The breadth of price increases supported the Bank’s judgment. Core measures had moved down to around 2%. The proportion of CPI components rising by more than 3% was close to its historical average. Food inflation was still high but moderating, and shelter inflation continued to ease. These observations give three distinct views of persistence: underlying price momentum, the number of categories with large increases, and the behaviour of particularly important household expenses. They did not rule out later pass-through from energy, since firms can initially absorb higher costs. They did help explain why a higher oil trajectory could change the near-term headline forecast without triggering an immediate hike.

The demand picture also argued against drawing a strong conclusion from one aggregate. Consumer spending rose 1.4% despite the GDP decline. Government spending fell unexpectedly, housing activity weakened and business investment remained soft. Imports rose strongly with inventory rebuilding while exports fell. A shipment of imported goods entering inventories can increase both imports and inventories, so the two components should be read together when diagnosing domestic activity. May employment rose, yet the level of employment had changed little since the start of the year. Unemployment at 6.6% remained inside the 6½%–7% range described by the Bank. The combination supported a potential return to growth from a weak first quarter without implying that slack would disappear quickly.

External conditions complicated the transmission. War-related energy and supply-chain disruptions were weighing on global growth, the US administration continued to propose tariffs and US consumption and AI investment remained relatively strong. Canadian financial conditions had nonetheless loosened since April, global equities were buoyant and bond yields were volatile. A weaker Canadian dollar against the US dollar and other currencies could affect local-currency import costs. The statement did not assign an inflation effect to that depreciation. Council’s commitment was to prevent energy inflation from becoming persistent. It specified neither a numerical oil threshold for action nor a sign that all firms were already passing through the shock. For a market researcher, the relevant update was the combination of prolonged cost exposure, weak demand and still-limited pricing breadth.

questions.question: Is the expected near-3% headline rate surviving outside fuel and the carbon-tax base effect?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the contributions of gasoline, other energy and the tax comparison, then track the bank’s core measures and the proportion of components exceeding 3%. Use consistent weights and vintages. If above-target readings stay concentrated as the tax base effect passes, they would carry different information from a widening distribution of large price increases.

questions.question: Is the second-quarter rebound evidence of stronger final demand?
questions.detail: Follow consumer and government outlays, non-residential investment, imports and inventories through the next GDP release. Separate inventory accumulation from sales to domestic end users and check employment and hours. A rebound driven by stock adjustment after a weak quarter would remove less slack than strength in final demand over several releases.

questions.question: Did currency depreciation amplify the domestic cost of higher oil?
questions.detail: Compare oil and imported-input prices in Canadian and foreign currency, alongside producer and consumer prices in fuel-intensive sectors. Check timing, hedging and whether firms reported margin compression. This would help judge how much cost pressure remained to be passed on at the June meeting without attributing every simultaneous movement in prices to the exchange rate. Changes in retail margins and the lag from imported fuel delivery to sale could help explain gaps between the cost and consumer price series.
